Question (original step 3):
Background Questions
How often do think about abortion or discuss it with others? How does this topic make you feel?
(Please write two or more sentences.)
Response:
I don't know that I think about or discuss it very often, though I certainly have done more of both since Roe v. Wade was overturned. Anyone around me with whom I would discuss it has the same views as I do---that it's free access is vital, that it is an issue of bodily autonomy that should not be interfered with by the state, that is it is not immoral or criminal, and that the life (both in terms of being alive, but also living a life that one wants) of an adult woman is vastly more important than the life or "rights" of a fetus. So I guess what I'm trying to say is that I don't discuss it much with those around me because there isn't much to say other than lamenting the injustice of having that right taken away from women. The idea of abortion, the act itself, does not bother me in the least. I've never had one, but I would not hesitate to do so were I to find myself pregnant as I do not want to have children. I would not feel bad about it, I would not mourn the unborn fetus, I would not agonize over the choice. I would treat it as I would, emotionally, any other medical intervention. The debate around it, however, makes me incredibly angry. Irate. Because the restrictions on it exist almost purely to control the lives of women, no matter how it is couched (generally in terms of religious objection). It is just a glaring example of the lack of respect for women's autonomy, for their position in the world as fully realized people and citizens. It is used to keep them in a position of subordinance, to oppress. Without access to abortion women will never truly be free to live in an actualized way.  

Question (original step 4):
Background Questions
Do you think abortion should be legal or illegal? Which circumstances does your answer depend on?
(Please write two or more sentences.)
Response:
Legal, without a doubt. It's illegality is baffling in the modern secular world. My answer does not depend on any circumstances at all: if a person wants an abortion they should be able to get one, full stop. Once the fetus becomes developed enough to be viable outside the womb---viable in the sense of being able to grow and thrive, not just survive while hooked to all amalgamation of tubes and contraptions---things certainly become murky. But my inclination will always be towards its full access and legality. If a person does not want to birth a child they should not be forced to.

Question (original step 5):
Background Questions
Where do your beliefs about abortion come from? For example, did particular life experiences influence your beliefs?
(Please write two or more sentences.)
Response:
My beliefs come from my lived experience as a human being. Freedom is vital to every living creature. The idea that someone can delineate to me exactly what decisions I am allowed to make concerning the only thing that is truly mine---my body, my corporeal self---is an anathema to me. I cannot stand it, it makes me want grit my teeth into dust, it makes me so angry. No man would consent to the amount of restrictions placed upon a woman's autonomy, both as it existed in the past and in today's world. Any person who does not believe in the free access of abortion to women does not believe women are fully-formed, thinking, feeling, breathing creatures just as themselves. They believe they are other in some way and must be treated as such. 

Question (original step 6):
Background Questions
Can you describe a situation where you are not sure if abortion is appropriate or not? If so, what makes this situation borderline or unclear?
(Please write two or more sentences.)
Response:
Almost none, truly. Abortion is appropriate in basically any situation in which a woman has decided she needs one. However,  as I said in another answer things do become more ethically ambiguous once the fetus is developed to such a degree as to basically be what be what we as a society consider an infant. As a person who believes in the rights of the child in an actual way (not in the way that those who oppose abortion will wield this point to act as evidence of their moral righteousness) then I must concede that at some point the fetus becomes a person, and a person has rights. But I think a woman's right to abortion should supersede that of a fetus is most scenarios. I lean closer to the belief that a fetus is not a person until it is born, though this is a point that I could think over philosophically for quite a while and never feel that I've settled the question.
